clinicalPearls: SPG45 is an autosomal recessive, early-onset complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in NT5C2, which encodes cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase II (cN-II), an enzyme of purine-nucleotide metabolism that is strongly expressed in the brain.
It typically presents in infancy or early childhood with delayed motor milestones that evolve into spastic paraplegia or spastic tetraplegia.
Global developmental delay and intellectual disability are consistent features, distinguishing SPG45 from the pure HSPs.
Additional signs may include optic atrophy or reduced visual acuity, nystagmus, dysarthria and fixed lower-limb contractures.
The disorder was first delineated in consanguineous pedigrees, so consanguinity or affected siblings supports the recessive diagnosis.
Neuroimaging can show thinning of the corpus callosum and white-matter change in some individuals, but may be relatively unremarkable.

The gene shows a striking context dependence: germline biallelic loss of NT5C2 causes SPG45, whereas somatically acquired activating NT5C2 mutations drive thiopurine resistance in relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
There is no disease-specific therapy; care is supportive, with spasticity management, developmental support, communication aids and physiotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG45 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in NT5C2 on chromosome 10q24, which encodes cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase II (cN-II). This enzyme dephosphorylates purine (and some pyrimidine) nucleoside monophosphates such as IMP and GMP and thereby helps to maintain the balance of intracellular nucleotide and nucleoside pools; it is highly expressed in the central nervous system. Loss of cN-II activity is thought to perturb neuronal purine-nucleotide homeostasis, and functional studies have linked NT5C2 deficiency to altered mTOR and ribosomal signalling and to impaired neuronal and axonal integrity, producing a length-dependent corticospinal axonopathy alongside a broader neurodevelopmental disturbance that accounts for the intellectual disability and other complicating features. The same gene displays a notable context dependence: germline loss of function underlies SPG45, whereas somatically acquired gain-of-function NT5C2 mutations confer thiopurine resistance in relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: SPG49 (TECPR2) and the AP-4-deficiency HSPs SPG47 (AP4B1), SPG50 (AP4M1), SPG51 (AP4E1) and SPG52 (AP4S1) - other recessive complicated childhood HSPs with intellectual disability and thin corpus callosum
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (ZFYVE26) - recessive HSP with thin corpus callosum and cognitive decline
Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy - the key mimic in a child with early spasticity
Leukodystrophies and inborn errors of metabolism presenting with spasticity and developmental delay
Treatable metabolic spastic paraplegias such as arginase deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing (HSP or neurodevelopmental gene panel, or exome sequencing) to identify biallelic NT5C2 variants
MRI of the brain and spine, looking for a thin corpus callosum and white-matter change and excluding structural causes
Ophthalmological review including optic-nerve assessment and visual acuity
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable inborn errors (plasma amino acids, very-long-chain fatty acids and related tests)
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography if amyotrophy or neuropathy is suspected
Parental testing and segregation analysis to confirm biallelic recessive inheritance
redFlags: Regression or loss of previously acquired skills - prompts a search for a metabolic or leukodystrophic cause
Progressive visual failure from optic atrophy - needs ophthalmology input and affects function and schooling
New seizures or rapidly worsening tone - reassess the diagnosis and imaging
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy accompanying hypertonia
reference.prognosis: SPG45 is an early-onset disorder combining intellectual disability with often significant motor disability; the spasticity is generally slowly progressive and lifespan is not necessarily shortened, but overall functional outcome is limited chiefly by the neurodevelopmental component.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early spasticity with developmental delay as non-progressive cerebral palsy and missing the genetic diagnosis with its recurrence risk.
Assuming a pure HSP - SPG45 is a complicated form and intellectual disability is expected.
Failing to confirm biallelic inheritance and segregation before counselling the family.
Confusing the germline loss-of-function role of NT5C2 with the unrelated somatic oncogenic mutations seen in relapsed leukaemia.
